caption:
Federal prosecutors say the former OpenAI engineer accused of bugging an executive conference room was in frequent WhatsApp contact with a Saudi royal.
The filing says the royal tried to recruit him, but it does not say the royal directed the device.
He faces a detention hearing in San Francisco and has not been convicted.

Should AI labs be guarded like national security sites?

Source: CNBC, Quartz · Photo: U.S. Department of Justice via Reuters

slides.headline: The OpenAI bugging suspect was texting a *Saudi royal* days before his arrest, feds say

image.credit: U.S. Department of Justice via Reuters

slides.heading: Texts with a *royal*
paras: Prosecutors say Abdulrahman Alfozan, the former OpenAI engineer accused of bugging an executive conference room, was in frequent WhatsApp contact with a Saudi royal in 2025 and 2026.
The royal is not named. Their most recent contact was on October 5, four days before his arrest.

slides.heading: A job offer *back home*
paras: The filing says the royal tried to recruit him to an AI initiative in Saudi Arabia. Alfozan allegedly agreed, but said he would not leave OpenAI until his stock vested.
Prosecutors do not say the royal directed the device or any theft of information.

slides.heading: Family flown to *Doha*
paras: Prosecutors say that after his arrest, travel arrangements linked to the Saudi government moved his wife and infant son out of the U.S. to Doha, Qatar, on October 10.
They want him held without bail and call him a flight risk.

slides.heading: His side of the *story*
paras: His lawyer, William Pernik, asks for home detention with GPS monitoring. He says Alfozan knew the device had been found 8 to 10 days before his arrest and did not flee.

paras.t: A detention hearing is set for Monday in federal court in San Francisco. He has not been convicted.

slides.hook: A spy case inside one of the world's top AI labs is still unfolding. Follow for what the judge decides.
